intro.title: prefers-color-scheme (dark mode)
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple webpage that automatically switches between light and dark themes based on your device's system settings. You will learn the core concept of the CSS media query `prefers-color-scheme`, which detects if a user prefers a light or dark color scheme. The main technology involved is CSS, using media queries to apply different styles for background colors, text colors, and other elements. By the end, you'll understand how to create a responsive design that respects user preferences for a better browsing experience.
intro.usecase: The prefers-color-scheme media query is essential for implementing dark mode across modern applications, enhancing user comfort and accessibility. Developers use it in dashboards, admin panels, and content-heavy sites like news readers or code editors to automatically switch themes based on system settings. This pattern is critical in settings panels, modals, and forms where consistent theming reduces eye strain and improves usability in low-light environments.

objectives: Apply the prefers-color-scheme media query to detect user system color preferences
Configure CSS custom properties (variables) for light and dark theme color values
Construct separate color schemes for light and dark modes using CSS rules
Implement a toggle mechanism to switch between color schemes manually
Integrate system preference detection with manual override functionality
Manipulate element styling based on active color scheme selection
Update existing CSS to use color variables instead of hard-coded values

steps.title: Create a CSS file and link it to HTML
steps.instruction: Create a new CSS file named 'styles.css' and link it to your HTML document using a <link> tag in the <head> section.
steps.hint: In your HTML file, add <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css"> inside the <head> element.
steps.expectedOutcome: A CSS file is created and properly linked to your HTML document, ready for styling.
successCriteria: A CSS file named 'styles.css' exists and is linked to HTML via a <link> tag in the <head> section.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've created a CSS file named 'styles.css' and linked it in the HTML <head> with <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">.
steps.feedbackWrong: create a CSS file and link it to your HTML. The <link> tag should be inside the <head> section of your HTML.

steps.title: Define base CSS variables for light mode
steps.instruction: Inside your CSS file, create a :root selector and define CSS custom properties (variables) for light mode colors. Include at least --background-color, --text-color, and --accent-color with appropriate light mode values.
steps.hint: The :root selector targets the highest-level parent element. Define variables using --variable-name: value; syntax. Use light colors like white, black, and a bright accent.
steps.expectedOutcome: The :root selector will contain CSS custom properties defining a light color scheme, ready to be used throughout the stylesheet.
successCriteria: The :root selector exists and contains at least three CSS custom properties (--background-color, --text-color, --accent-color) with light mode color values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started defining variables, but make sure you have at least --background-color, --text-color, and --accent-color with appropriate light colors inside the :root selector.
steps.feedbackWrong: The code doesn't match the requirements. You need to create a :root selector with CSS custom properties for light mode colors.

steps.title: Apply the light mode variables to elements
steps.instruction: Apply the CSS variables you defined to style the body, headings, and paragraphs to create a light-themed interface.
steps.hint: Use the var() function to reference your CSS variables. For example, to set the body background, use background-color: var(--background-color);
steps.expectedOutcome: The body, headings, and paragraphs will be styled using the CSS variables you defined, creating a light-themed interface.
successCriteria: CSS variables are applied to at least the body, headings, and paragraphs using the var() function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've applied some CSS variables, but make sure to style the body, headings, and paragraphs.
steps.feedbackWrong: The CSS variables aren't applied correctly. Use the var() function to reference your variables for styling.

steps.title: Introduce the prefers-color-scheme media query
steps.instruction: Add a media query using @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) to target devices that have dark mode enabled in their system settings.
steps.hint: Use the @media rule with (prefers-color-scheme: dark) to create a section for dark mode styles. Place it after your existing light mode styles.
steps.expectedOutcome: A media query targeting dark mode system preferences is added to the CSS file.
successCriteria: The CSS contains @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) with an empty rule block.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the exact syntax @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) with curly braces.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to add a media query using @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {}.

steps.title: Define dark mode CSS variables inside the media query
steps.instruction: Inside the @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) block, redefine the same CSS variables with dark mode color values (e.g., dark background, light text).
steps.hint: You'll need to override the CSS variables you defined earlier by setting new values inside the media query block.
steps.expectedOutcome: The CSS file will contain a @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) block with redefined CSS variables for dark mode colors.
successCriteria: The @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) block contains CSS variable definitions with dark mode color values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added the media query block, but make sure to redefine the CSS variables with appropriate dark mode colors inside it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires defining dark mode CSS variables inside the @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) block. Check if you've added the variable definitions with dark colors.

steps.title: Test the automatic dark mode switch
steps.instruction: Open your browser's developer tools and change the system color scheme preference to dark mode,
steps.hint: In Chrome or Firefox dev tools, find the 'Toggle device toolbar' and look for a 'prefers-color-scheme' emulation option to switch between light and dark modes.
steps.analogousExample:
/* Testing a media query effect */
/* Change your system's dark mode setting and reload the page */
steps.expectedOutcome: When you switch your system to dark mode and reload, the page should automatically use the dark mode colors defined in your media query.
successCriteria: You have tested the dark mode switch by changing your system preference and reloading the page.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you've actually changed your system's color scheme preference to dark mode and reloaded the page to see the effect.
steps.feedbackWrong: The test didn't work as expected. Check that you've properly defined dark mode variables inside the @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) query and that you've actually switched your system to dark mode before reloading.

steps.hint: In Chrome or Firefox dev tools, find the 'Toggle device toolbar' and look for a 'prefers-color-scheme' emulation option to switch between light and dark modes.
steps.analogousExample:

steps.feedbackPartial: Review the instruction and try again.

steps.title: Add a toggle switch element in HTML
steps.instruction: Add a checkbox input element with an id of 'theme-toggle' and a label for it in your HTML file.
steps.hint: You need to add HTML markup, not CSS. Create a checkbox input with id='theme-toggle' and a label element with for='theme-toggle'.
steps.analogousExample:
<!-- Example: a checkbox with label -->
<input type="checkbox" id="example-toggle">
<label for="example-toggle">Toggle me</label>
steps.expectedOutcome: Your HTML file will contain a checkbox input with id='theme-toggle' and a corresponding label element.
successCriteria: The HTML contains an <input type="checkbox" id="theme-toggle"> element and a <label for="theme-toggle"> element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some HTML, but make sure you have both the checkbox input with id='theme-toggle' and a label element with for='theme-toggle'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The HTML toggle switch elements are missing or incorrect. Add a checkbox input with id='theme-toggle' and a label for it.

steps.title: Style the toggle switch with CSS
steps.instruction: Add CSS rules to style the toggle switch element you created in the HTML. Target it by its ID or class and set properties like width, height, background-color, border-radius, and position to make it visually appealing.
steps.hint: Use a selector like #theme-toggle or .toggle-switch, then add CSS properties inside curly braces. Set width and height to control size, background-color for the switch color, and border-radius to make it rounded.
steps.expectedOutcome: The toggle switch element in your HTML will have basic visual styling applied, such as a specific size, color, and shape.
successCriteria: CSS rules are added that target the toggle switch element and include at least three styling properties (e.g., width, height, background-color, border-radius).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some styling, but make sure to include at least three different CSS properties (like width, height, and background-color) to fully style the toggle switch.
steps.feedbackWrong: The toggle switch styling is missing or incomplete. Add CSS rules that target the toggle switch element and set multiple visual properties.

steps.title: Use the :checked pseudo-class to define manual dark mode
steps.instruction: Add a CSS rule that uses the :checked pseudo-class selector on the toggle switch to apply dark mode CSS variables when the switch is checked, overriding the prefers-color-scheme media query.
steps.hint: Target the toggle switch checkbox with its ID and the :checked pseudo-class, then set the same dark mode CSS variables you defined earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: The CSS will include a rule that applies dark mode styles when the toggle switch is checked, allowing manual override of the system preference.
successCriteria: A CSS rule with the :checked pseudo-class selector is added, targeting the toggle switch and setting dark mode CSS variables.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the correct selector and setting the dark mode CSS variables inside the :checked rule.
steps.feedbackWrong: The :checked rule is missing or incorrect. Remember to target the toggle switch checkbox with its ID and the :checked pseudo-class, then apply the dark mode CSS variables.

steps.title: Test the manual override functionality
steps.instruction: Test your page by toggling the switch on/off and changing your system color scheme preference to verify both automatic (prefers-color-scheme) and manual (toggle switch) dark mode work correctly.
steps.hint: Open your HTML file in a browser, toggle the switch you styled, and change your system's dark/light mode setting to see the transitions.
steps.expectedOutcome: You should see the page switch between light and dark themes both when you toggle the switch and when you change your system's color scheme preference.
successCriteria: Both automatic (via prefers-color-scheme) and manual (via toggle switch) dark mode switching work correctly.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure both the toggle switch and system preference changes trigger the theme switch.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that your CSS variables, media query, and :checked rule are correctly defined and applied.
